newsitem.title: USA: IPO SPOTLIGHT - Ticketmaster boosted by name value.
newsitem.headline: IPO SPOTLIGHT - Ticketmaster boosted by name value.

text.p: Ticketmaster Group Inc's initial public offering is seen rising modestly at its debut on the strength of its well-known name, despite company debt and the controversy sparked by the rock group Pearl Jam.
The IPO is expected to price Monday evening or Tuesday, in a range of $13 to $15 per common stock.

"Ticketmaster will probably do well, mostly based on its solid name recognition, but they're going to have to put on blinders as to its financials," said David Menlow, president of the IPO Financial Network, based in Springfield, N.J.
"Still the deal should do well based on the company's notoriety," Menlow added.

Ticketmaster Group, a Los Angeles-based provider of automated ticketing services in the U.S., is majority owned by Paul Allen, a co-founder of Microsoft Corp. Allen serves as a director and chairman of the board.
"I don't think it is great because the company really has lots of debt," said Manish Shah, editor of the IPO Maven.
"But I think it could do well. It's a very well-known company," Shah said. "It might have an opening pop, but I don't think more than $1 to $1.50."
As a result of its growth and cash distributions, Ticketmaster incurred long-term debt and is highly leveraged.

As of July 31, 1996, the company had consolidated long-term debt of $183.6 million, according to the company's financial statements. For the six months to July 31, 1996, Ticketmaster reported a net income loss of $2.4 million, or $0.16 per share.

In 1995, the Justice Department closed an investigation, initiated by complaints from the Seattle-based alternative rock band Pearl Jam, alleging Ticketmaster monopolized the ticketing market for concerts and sporting events.

The Justice Department cited competition in the ticketing industry, represented by companies such as Fans, Tours & Tickets (FT&T) and ETM Entertainment Network Inc, which also designs and operates electronic networks for ticketing.

For its 1996 fall tour, the Grammy Award-winning Pearl Jam selected FT&T, a division of the Philadelphia-based merchant bank Fillmore Mercantile, to arrange ticketing services, a spokeswoman for Sony Corp's EPIC label said.

Ticketmaster sold 53.1 million tickets in fiscal 1996, generating revenues of $241.3 million, according to the company's financial statements. Comparable figures for its privately-held competitors were not available.
The company is planning to offer 7.25 million shares, with shares trading on the Nasdaq under the symbol "TKTM."
It plans to use proceeds to retire debt and for general corporate purposes.
Allen & Co Inc, Lazard Freres & Co LCC and Smith Barney Inc are underwriters of the stock sale.
